plain_english: "I'm upset that people pity me," someone says. So is being pitied something that concerns you or the people who pity you? Well, can you stop this pity? Yes, I can — if I show them I don't need their pity. So are you actually in a condition that deserves pity, or aren't you? I don't think I am. But these people don't pity me for the right reasons. If they're going to pity me, it should be for my character flaws. Instead, they pity me for my poverty, for not having important jobs, for sickness and death and things like that.
original_excerpt: I am grieved, a man says, at being pitied. Whether then is the fact of your being pitied a thing which concerns you or those who pity you? Well, is it in your power to stop this pity? It is in my power, if I show them that I do not require pity. And whether then are you in the condition of not deserving (requiring) pity, or are you not in that condition? I think that I am not; but these persons do not pity me, for the things for which, if they ought to pity me, it would be proper, I mean, for my faults; but they pity me for my poverty, for not possessing honorable offices, for diseases and deaths and other such things.
source_reference: Discourses, Against Those Who Lament Over Being Pitied

plain_english: So are you ready to convince people that none of these things are actually bad — that someone can be happy even if they're poor, powerless, and unknown? Or would you rather just show off wealth and status to impress them? The second option is for people who are show-offs, fools, and worthless. And think about what you'd have to do to keep up that fake image.
original_excerpt: Whether then are you prepared to convince the many, that not one of these things is an evil, but that it is possible for a man who is poor and has no office ([Greek: anarchonti)] and enjoys no honor to be happy; or to show yourself to them as rich and in power? For the second of these things belong to a man who is boastful, silly, and good for nothing. And consider by what means the pretence must be supported.
source_reference: Discourses, Against Those Who Lament Over Being Pitied

plain_english: You'll need to hire slaves and own some silver dishes. You'll have to show them off in public — using the same ones over and over if you have to, while trying to hide that fact. You'll need fancy clothes and other things just for show. You'll have to make people think the important folks respect you. You'll try to eat dinner at their houses, or at least make people think you do. And you'll use cheap tricks to make yourself look better and more noble than you really are. This is what you'll have to do if you choose the second path — the one where you avoid being pitied.
original_excerpt: It will be necessary for you to hire slaves and to possess a few silver vessels, and to exhibit them in public, if it is possible, though they are often the same, and to attempt to conceal the fact that they are the same, and to have splendid garments, and all other things for display, and to show that you are a man honored by the great, and to try to sup at their houses, or to be supposed to sup there, and as to your person to employ some mean arts, that you may appear to be more handsome and nobler than you are. These things you must contrive, if you choose to go by the second path in order not to be pitied.
source_reference: Discourses, Against Those Who Lament Over Being Pitied

plain_english: The first approach is impossible and takes forever. You're trying to do something even Zeus couldn't do — convince everyone what's good and bad. Do you have that power? No. You only have the power to convince yourself. And you haven't even done that yet. So why are you trying to persuade other people? Who has spent more time with you than you have with yourself? Who has more influence over you than you do? Who cares more about you than you do? So why haven't you convinced yourself to learn yet?
original_excerpt: But the first way is both impracticable and long, to attempt the very thing which Zeus has not been able to do, to convince all men what things are good and bad. Is this power given to you? This only is given to you, to convince yourself; and you have not convinced yourself. Then I ask you, do you attempt to persuade other men? and who has lived so long with you as you with yourself? and who has so much power of convincing you as you have of convincing yourself; and who is better disposed and nearer to you than you are to yourself? How then have you not yet convinced yourself in order to learn?
source_reference: Discourses, Against Those Who Lament Over Being Pitied

plain_english: Aren't things backwards right now? Is this what you've been working so hard to do — to learn how to be free from grief and worry, to not feel defeated, to be truly free? Haven't you heard there's only one way to reach this goal? Give up the things that aren't under your control. Step back from them. Accept that they belong to other people. So when someone has an opinion about you — what kind of thing is that? It's not under your control. So it's nothing to you. It's nothing. But when you're still upset and bothered by it, do you really think you understand what's good and what's bad?
original_excerpt: At present are not things upside down? Is this what you have been earnest about doing, to learn to be free from grief and free from disturbance, and not to be humbled (abject), and to be free? Have you not heard then that there is only one way which leads to this end, to give up (dismiss) the things which do not depend on the will, to withdraw from them, and to admit that they belong to others? For another man then to have an opinion about you, of what kind is it? It is a thing independent of the will—Then is it nothing to you? It is nothing. When then you are still vexed at this and disturbed, do you think that you are convinced about good and evil?
source_reference: Discourses, Against Those Who Lament Over Being Pitied
